when her waves do roar like great waters, a noise of their voice is uttered: <hi type="super">56</hi> Because the spoiler is come upon her, <hi type="italic">even</hi> upon Babylon, and her mighty men are taken, every one of their bows is broken: for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of recompences shall surely requite. <hi type="super">57</hi> And I will make drunk her princes, and her wise <hi type="italic">men,</hi> her captains, and her rulers, and her mighty men: and they shall sleep a perpetual sleep, and not wake, saith the King, whose name <hi type="italic">is</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts. <hi type="super">58</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts; The broad walls of Babylon shall be utterly broken, and her high gates shall be burned with fire; and the people shall labour in vain, and the folk in the fire, and they shall be weary. <div eID="gen18212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18213" type="x-p"/> The particulars of this copious prophecy are dispersed and interwoven, and the same things left and returned to so often that it could not well be divided into parts, but we must endeavor to collect them under their proper heads. Let us then observe here, <div eID="gen18213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18214" type="x-p"/> I. An acknowledgment of the great pomp and power that Babylon had been in and the use that God in his providence had made of it (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">Babylon hath been a golden cup,</hi> a rich and glorious empire, <hi type="italic">a golden city</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.4">Isa. xiv. 4</reference>), <hi type="italic">a head of gold</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.38">Dan. ii. 38</reference>), filled with all good things, as a cup with wine. Nay, she had been <hi type="italic">a golden cup in the Lord's hand;</hi> he had in a particular manner filled and favoured her with blessings; he had made the earth <hi type="italic">drunk with this cup;</hi> some were intoxicated with her pleasures and debauched by her, others intoxicated with her terrors and destroyed by her. In both senses the New-Testament Babylon is said to have made the kings of the earth drunk, <reference osisRef="Rev.17.2">Rev. xvii. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.18.3">xviii. 3</reference>. Babylon had also been God's <hi type="italic">battle-axe;</hi> it was so at this time, when Jeremiah prophesied, and was likely to be yet more so, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.20">v. 20</reference>. The forces of Babylon were God's <hi type="italic">weapons of war,</hi> tools in his hand, with which he broke in pieces, and knocked down, <hi type="italic">nations and kingdoms,</hi>—<hi type="italic">horses</hi> and <hi type="italic">chariots,</hi> which are so much the strength of kingdoms (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.21">v. 21</reference>),—<hi type="italic">man and woman, young and old,</hi> with which kingdoms are replenished (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.22">v. 22</reference>),—<hi type="italic">the shepherd and his flock, the husbandman and his oxen,</hi> with which kingdoms are maintained and supplied, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.23">v. 23</reference>. Such havoc as this the Chaldeans had made when God employed them as instruments of his wrath for the chastising of the nations; and yet now Babylon itself must fall. Note, Those that have carried all before them a great while will yet at length meet with their match, and their day also will come to fall; the rod will itself be thrown into the fire at last. Nor can any think it will exempt them from God's judgments that they have been instrumental in executing his judgments on others. <div eID="gen18214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18215" type="x-p"/> II. A just complaint made of Babylon, and a charge drawn up against her by the Israel of God. 1. She is complained of for her incorrigible wickedness (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">We would have healed Babylon, but she is not healed.</hi> The people of God that were captives among the Babylonians endeavoured, according to the instructions given them (<reference osisRef="Jer.10.11">Jer. x. 11</reference>), to convince them of the folly of their idolatry, but they could not do it; still they doted as much as ever upon their graven images, and therefore the Israelites resolved to quit them and go to their own country. Yet some understand this as spoken by the forces they had hired for their assistance, declaring that they had done their best to save her from ruin, but that it was all to no purpose, and therefore they might as well go home to their respective countries; "for <hi type="italic">her judgment reaches unto heaven,</hi> and it is in vain to withstand it or think to avert it." 2. She is complained of for her inveterate malice against Israel. Other nations had been hardly used by the Chaldeans, but Israel only complains to God of it, and with confidence appeals to him (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.34-Jer.51.35">v. 34, 35</reference>): "<hi type="italic">The king of Babylon has devoured me, and crushed me,</hi> and never thought he could do enough ruin to me; <hi type="italic">he has emptied me</hi> of all that was valuable, has <hi type="italic">swallowed me up as a dragon,</hi> or whale, swallows up the little fish by shoals; <hi type="italic">he has filled his belly,</hi> filled his treasures, <hi type="italic">with my delicates,</hi> with all my pleasant things, <hi type="italic">and has cast me out,</hi> cast me away as a <hi type="italic">vessel in which there is no pleasure;</hi> and now let them be accountable for all this." <hi type="italic">Zion and Jerusalem shall say,</hi> "Let <hi type="italic">the violence done to me and</hi> my children, that are <hi type="italic">my</hi> own <hi type="italic">flesh,</hi> and pieces of myself, and all the blood of my people, which they have shed like water, <hi type="italic">be upon</hi> them; let the guilt of it lie upon them, and let it be required at their hands." Note, Ruin is not far off from those that lie under the guilt of wrong done to God's people. <div eID="gen18215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18216" type="x-p"/> III. Judgment given upon this appeal by the righteous Judge of heaven and earth, on behalf of Israel against Babylon. He <hi type="italic">sits in the throne judging right,</hi> is ready to receive complaints, and answers (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.36">v. 36</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I will plead thy cause.</hi> Leave it with me; I will in due time plead it effectually <hi type="italic">and take vengeance for thee,</hi> and every drop of Jerusalem's blood shall be accounted for with interest." Israel and Judah seemed to have been neglected and forgotten, but God had an eye to them, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.5">v. 5</reference>. It is true <hi type="italic">their land was filled with sin against the Holy One of Israel.</hi> They were a provoking people and their sins were a great offence to God, as a holy God, and as their God, their Holy One; and therefore he justly delivered them up into the hands of their enemies, and might justly have abandoned them and left them to perish in their hands; but God deals better with them than they deserve, and, notwithstanding their iniquities and his severities, <hi type="italic">Israel is not forsaken,</hi> is not cast off, though he be cast out, but is owned and looked after by his God, by the Lord of hosts. God is his God still, and will act for him as the Lord of hosts, a God of power. Note, Though God's people may have broken his laws and fallen under his rebukes, yet it does not therefore follow that they are thrown out of covenant; but God's care of them and love to them will <hi type="italic">flourish again,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.89.30-Ps.89.33">Ps. lxxxix. 30-33</reference>. The Chaldeans thought they should never be called to an account for what they had done against God's Israel; but there is <hi type="italic">a time</hi> fixed <hi type="italic">for vengeance,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.51.6">v. 6</reference>. We cannot expect it should come sooner than the time fixed, but then it will come; he <hi type="italic">will render unto Babylon a recompence,</hi> for the avenging of Israel is <hi type="italic">the vengeance of the Lord,</hi> who espouses their cause; it is <hi type="italic">the vengeance of his temple,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.51.11">v. 11</reference>, as before, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.28">ch. l. 28</reference>. <hi type="italic">The Lord God of recompences,</hi> the <hi type="italic">God to whom vengeance belongs, will surely requite</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.56">v. 56</reference>), will pay them home; he will <hi type="italic">render unto Babylon all the evil they have done in Zion</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.24">v. 24</reference>); he will return it <hi type="italic">in the sight</hi> of his people. They shall have the satisfaction to see their cause pleaded with jealousy. They shall not only live to see those judgments brought upon Babylon, but they shall plainly see them to be the punishment of the wrong they have done to Zion; any man may see it, and say, <hi type="italic">Verily there is a God that judges in the earth;</hi> for just as <hi type="italic">Babylon has caused the slain of Israel to fall,</hi> has not only slain those that were found in arms, but all without distinction, even <hi type="italic">all the land</hi> (almost all were put to the sword), so <hi type="italic">at Babylon shall fall</hi> the slain not only of the city, but of <hi type="italic">all the country,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.51.49">v. 49</reference>. Cyrus shall measure to the Chaldeans the same that they measured to the Jews, so that every observer may discern that God is recompensing them for what they did against his people; but Zion's children shall in a particular manner triumph in it (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord has brought forth our righteousness;</hi> he has appeared in our behalf against those that dealt unjustly with us, and has given us redress; he has also made it to appear that he is reconciled to us and that we are yet in his eyes a <hi type="italic">righteous nation.</hi> Let it therefore be spoken of to his praise: <hi type="italic">Come and let us declare in Zion the work of the Lord our God,</hi> that others may be invited to join with us in praising him. <div eID="gen18216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18217" type="x-p"/> IV. A declaration of the greatness and sovereignty of that God who espouses Zion's cause and undertakes to reckon with this proud and potent enemy, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.14">v. 14</reference>. It is <hi type="italic">the Lord of hosts</hi> that has said it, that has <hi type="italic">sworn it,</hi> has <hi type="italic">sworn it by himself</hi> (for he could swear by no greater), that he will fill Babylon with vast and incredible numbers of the enemy's forces, will <hi type="italic">fill it with men as with caterpillars,</hi> that shall overpower it will multitudes, and need only to <hi type="italic">lift up a shout</hi> against it, for that shall be so terrible as to dispirit all the inhabitants and make them an easy prey to this numerous army. But who, and where, is he that can break so powerful a kingdom as Babylon? The prophet gives an account of him from the description he had formerly given of him, and of his sovereignty and victory over all pretenders (<reference osisRef="Jer.10.12-Jer.10.16">Jer. x. 12-16</reference>), which was there intended for the conviction of the Babylonian idolaters and the confirmation of God's Israel in the faith and worship of the God of Israel; and it is here repeated to show that God will convince those by his judgments who would not be convinced by his word that he is <hi type="italic">God over all.</hi> Let not any doubt but that he who has determined to destroy Babylon is able to make his words good, for, 1. He is the God that made the world (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.15">v. 15</reference>), and therefore nothing is too hard for him to do; it is in his name that our help stands, and on him our hope is built. 2. He has the command of all the creatures that he has made (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.16">v. 16</reference>); his providence is a continued creation. He has <hi type="italic">wind and rain</hi> at his disposal. If he speak the word, there is a <hi type="italic">multitude of waters in the heavens</hi> (and it is a wonder how they hang there), fed by <hi type="italic">vapours out of the earth,</hi> and it is a wonder how they ascend thence. <hi type="italic">Lightnings and rain</hi> seem contraries, as fire and water, and yet they are produced together; and the wind, which seems arbitrary in its motions, and we <hi type="italic">know not whence it comes,</hi> is yet, we are sure, brought <hi type="italic">out of his treasuries.</hi> 3. The idols that oppose the accomplishment of his word are a mere sham and their worshippers brutish people, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.17-Jer.51.18">v. 17, 18</reference>. The idols are falsehood, they are vanity, they are <hi type="italic">the work of errors;</hi> when they come to be visited (to be examined and enquired into) <hi type="italic">they perish,</hi> that is, their reputation sinks and they appear to be nothing; and those <hi type="italic">that make them are like unto them.</hi> But between the God of Israel and these gods of the heathen there is no comparison (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">The portion of Jacob is not like them;</hi> the God who speaks this and will do it is the <hi type="italic">former of all things</hi> and <hi type="italic">the Lord of all hosts,</hi> and therefore can do what he will; and there is a near relation between him and his people, for he is <hi type="italic">their portion</hi> and they are his; they put a confidence in him as their portion and he is pleased to take a complacency in them and a particular care of them as the <hi type="italic">lot of his inheritance;</hi> and therefore he will do what is best for them. The repetition of these things here, which were said before, intimates both the certainty and the importance of them, and obliges us to take special notice of them; <hi type="italic">God hath spoken once; yea, twice have we heard this, that power belongs to God,</hi> power to destroy the most formidable enemies of his church; and if God thus <hi type="italic">speak once, yea, twice,</hi> we are inexcusable if we do not perceive it and attend to it. <div eID="gen18217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18218" type="x-p"/> V. A description of the instruments that are to be employed in this service. God has <hi type="italic">raised up the spirit of the kings of the Medes</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.11">v. 11</reference>), Darius and Cyrus, who come against Babylon by a divine instinct; for <hi type="italic">God's device is against Babylon to destroy it.</hi> They do it, but God devised it, he designed it; they are but accomplishing his purpose, and acting as he directed. Note, God's counsel shall stand, and according to it all hearts shall move. Those whom God employs against Babylon are compared (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.1">v. 1</reference>) to a <hi type="italic">destroying wind,</hi> which either by its coldness blasts the fruits of the earth or by its fierceness blows down all before it. This wind is <hi type="italic">brought out of God's treasuries</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.16">v. 16</reference>), and it is here said to be <hi type="italic">raised up against those that dwell in the midst of the Chaldeans,</hi> those of other nations that inhabit among them and are incorporated with them. The Chaldeans rise up against God by falling down before idols, and against them God will raise up destroyers, for he will be too hard for those that contend with him. These enemies are compared to fanners (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.2">v. 2</reference>), who shall <hi type="italic">drive them away as chaff</hi> is driven away by the fan. The Chaldeans had been fanners to winnow God's people (<reference osisRef="Jer.15.7">ch. xv. 7</reference>) and to empty them, and now they shall themselves be in like manner despoiled and dispersed. <div eID="gen18218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18219" type="x-p"/> VI. An ample commission given them to destroy and lay all waste. Let them <hi type="italic">bend their bow</hi> against the archers of the Chaldeans (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.3">v. 3</reference>) and <hi type="italic">not spare her young men,</hi> but <hi type="italic">utterly destroy them,</hi> for the Lord has <hi type="italic">both devised and done what he spoke against Babylon,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.51.12">v. 12</reference>. This may animate the instruments he employs, but assuring them of success. The methods they take are such as God has devised and therefore they shall surely prosper; what he has spoken shall be done, for he himself will do it; and therefore let all necessary preparations be made. This they are called to, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.27-Jer.51.28">v. 27, 28</reference>. Let <hi type="italic">a standard be set up,</hi> under which to enlist soldiers for this expedition; <hi type="italic">let a trumpet be blown</hi> to call men together to it and animate them in it; let the nations, out of which Cyrus's army is to be raised, prepare their recruits; let the kingdoms of <hi type="italic">Ararat,</hi> and <hi type="italic">Minni, and Ashkenaz,</hi> of Armenia, both the higher and the lower, and of Ascania, about Phrygia and Bithynia, send in their quota of men for his service; let general officers be appointed and the cavalry advance; let the horses come up in <hi type="italic">great numbers,</hi> as the <hi type="italic">caterpillars,</hi> and come, like them, leaping and pawing in the valley; let them lay the country waste, as <hi type="italic">caterpillars</hi> do (<reference osisRef="Joel.1.4">Joel i. 4</reference>), especially rough caterpillars; let the kings and captains prepare nations against Babylon, for the service is great and there is occasion for many hands to be employed it. <div eID="gen18219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18220" type="x-p"/> VII. The weakness of the Chaldeans, and their inability to make head against this threatening destroying force. When God employed them against other nations they had spirit and strength to act offensively, and went on with admirable resolution, conquering and to conquer; but now that it comes to their turn to be reckoned with all their might and courage are gone, their hearts fail them, and none of all their men of might and mettle have found their hands to act so much as defensively. They are called upon here to prepare for action, but it is ironically and in an upbraiding way (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">Make bright the arrows,</hi> which have grown rusty through disuse; <hi type="italic">gather the shields,</hi> which in a long time of peace and security have been scattered and thrown out of the way (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.12">v. 12</reference>); <hi type="italic">set up the standard upon the walls of Babylon,</hi> upon the towers on those walls, to summon all that owed suit and service to that mother-city, now to come in to her assistance; let them make the watch as strong as they can, and appoint the sentinels to their respective posts, and prepare ambushes for the reception of the enemy. This intimates that they would be found very secure and remiss, and would need to be thus quickened (and they were so to such a degree that they were in the midst of their revels when the city was taken), but that all their preparations should come to no purpose. Whoever will may call them to it, but they shall have no heart to come at the call, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.29">v. 29</reference>. <hi type="italic">The</hi> whole <hi type="italic">land shall tremble, and sorrow</hi> (a universal consternation) shall seize upon them; for they shall see both the irresistible arm and the irreversible counsel and decree of God against them. They shall see that God is making <hi type="italic">Babylon a desolation,</hi> and therein is performing what he has purposed; and then <hi type="italic">the mighty men of Babylon have forborne to fight,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.51.30">v. 30</reference>. God having taken away their strength and spirit, so that they have <hi type="italic">remained in their holds,</hi> not daring so much as to peep forth, the might both of their hearts and of their hands fails; they <hi type="italic">become</hi> as timorous <hi type="italic">as women,</hi> so that the enemy has, without any resistance, <hi type="italic">burnt her dwelling-places</hi> and <hi type="italic">broken her bars.</hi> It is to the same purport with <reference osisRef="Jer.51.56-Jer.51.58">v. 56-58</reference>. When the spoiler comes upon Babylon her mighty men, who should make head against him, are immediately taken, their weapons of war fail them, <hi type="italic">every one of their bows is broken</hi> and stands them in no stead. Their politics fail them; they call councils of war, but their princes and captains, who sit in council to concert measures for the common safety, are made drunk; they are as men intoxicated through stupidity or despair; they can form no right notions of things; they stagger and are unsteady in their counsels and resolves, and dash one against another, and, like drunken men, fall out among themselves. At length they <hi type="italic">sleep a perpetual sleep,</hi> and never <hi type="italic">awake</hi> from their wine, the wine of God's wrath, for it is to them an opiate that lays them into a fatal lethargy. The <hi type="italic">walls of their city</hi> fail them, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.58">v. 58</reference>. When the enemy had found ways to ford Euphrates, which was thought impassable, yet surely, think they, the walls are impregnable, they are <hi type="italic">the broad walls of Babylon</hi> or (as the margin reads it), <hi type="italic">the walls of broad Babylon.</hi> The compass of the city, within the walls, was 385 furlongs, some say 480, that is, about sixty miles; the walls were 200 cubits high, and fifty cubits broad, so that two chariots might easily pass by one another upon them. Some say that there was a threefold wall about the inner city and the like about the outer, and that the stones of the wall, being laid in pitch instead of mortar (<reference osisRef="Gen.11.3">Gen. xi. 3</reference>), were scarcely separable; and yet these shall be <hi type="italic">utterly broken,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the high gates and towers shall be burnt,</hi> and the people that are employed in the defence of the city shall <hi type="italic">labour in vain in the fire;</hi> they shall quite tire themselves, but shall do no good. <div eID="gen18220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18221" type="x-p"/> VIII. The destruction that shall be made of Babylon by these invaders. 1. It is a certain destruction; the doom has passed and it cannot be reversed; a divine power is engaged against it, which cannot be resisted (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Babylon is fallen and destroyed,</hi> is as sure to fall, to fall into destruction, as if it were fallen and destroyed already; though when Jeremiah prophesied this, and many a year after, it was in the height of its power and greatness. God declares, God appears against Babylon (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.25">v. 25</reference>): <hi type="italic">Behold, I am against thee;</hi> and those cannot stand long whom God is against. He will <hi type="italic">stretch out his hand upon it,</hi> a hand which no creature can bear the weight of nor withstand the force of. It is his purpose, which shall be performed, that <hi type="italic">Babylon</hi> must be a <hi type="italic">desolation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.51.29">v. 29</reference>. 2. It is a righteous destruction. Babylon has made herself meet for it, and therefore cannot fail to meet with it. For (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.25">v. 25</reference>) <hi type="italic">Babylon</hi> has been <hi type="italic">a destroying mountain,</hi> very lofty and bulky as a mountain, and <hi type="italic">destroying all the earth,</hi> as the stones that are tumbled from high mountains spoil the grounds about them; but now it shall itself be <hi type="italic">rolled down from its rocks,</hi> which were as the foundations on which it stood. It shall be levelled, its pomp and power broken. It is now a burning mountain, like Ætna and the other volcanoes, that throw out fire, to the terror of all about them. But it shall be a burnt mountain; it shall at length have consumed itself, and shall remain a heap of ashes. So will this world be at the end of time. Again (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.33">v. 33</reference>), "<hi type="italic">Babylon is like a threshing-floor,</hi> in which the people of God have been long threshed, as sheaves in the floor; but now the time has come that she shall herself be threshed and her sheaves in her; her princes and great men, and all her inhabitants, shall be beaten in their own land, as in the threshing-floor. The threshing-floor is prepared. Babylon is by sin made meet to be a seat of war, and her people, like corn in harvest, are ripe for destruction," <reference osisRef="Rev.14.15">Rev. xiv. 15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.4.12">Mic. iv. 12</reference>. 3. It is an unavoidable destruction. Babylon seems to be well-fenced and fortified against it: <hi type="italic">She dwells upon many waters</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.13">v. 13</reference>); the situation of her country is such that it seems inaccessible, it is so surrounded, and the march of an enemy into it so embarrassed, by rivers. In allusion to this, the New-Testament Babylon is said to <hi type="italic">sit upon many waters,</hi> that is, to rule over many nations, as the other Babylon did, <reference osisRef="Rev.17.15">Rev. xvii. 15</reference>. <hi type="italic">Babylon is abundant in treasures;</hi> and yet "<hi type="italic">thy end has come,</hi> and neither they waters nor thy wealth shall secure thee." This end that comes shall be <hi type="italic">the measure of thy covetousness;</hi> it shall be the stint of thy gettings, it shall set bounds to thy ambition and avarice, which otherwise would have ben boundless. God, by the destruction of Babylon, said to its proud waves, <hi type="italic">Hitherto shall you come, and no further.</hi> Note, if men will not set a measure to their covetousness by wisdom and grace, God will set a measure to it by his judgments. Babylon, thinking herself very safe and very great, was very proud; but she will be deceived (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.53">v. 53</reference>): <hi type="italic">Though Babylon should mount</hi> her walls and palaces <hi type="italic">up to heaven,</hi> and though (because what is high is apt to totter) she should take care to <hi type="italic">fortify the height of her strength,</hi> yet all will not do; God will send spoilers against her, that shall break through her strength and bring down her height. 4. It is a gradual destruction, which, if they had pleased, they might have foreseen and had warning of; for (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.46">v. 46</reference>) "<hi type="italic">A rumor will come one year</hi> that Cyrus is making vast preparations for war, <hi type="italic">and after that, in another year, shall come a rumour</hi> that his design is upon Babylon, and he is steering his course that way;" so that when he was a great way off they might have sent and desired conditions of peace; but they were too proud, too secure, to do that, and their hearts were hardened to their destruction. 5. Yet, when it comes, it is a surprising destruction: <hi type="italic">Babylon has suddenly fallen</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.8">v. 8</reference>); the destruction came upon them when they did not think of it and was perfected in a little time, as that of the New-Testament <hi type="italic">Babylon—in one hour,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.18.17">Rev. xviii. 17</reference>. The king of Babylon, who should have been observing the approaches of the enemy, was himself at such a distance from the place where the attack was made that it was a great while ere he had notice that the city was taken; so that those who were posted near the place sent one messenger, one courier, after another, with advice of it, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.31">v. 31</reference>. The foot-posts shall meet at the court from several quarters with this intelligence to the king of Babylon that his <hi type="italic">city is taken at one end,</hi> and there is nothing to obstruct the progress of the conquerors, but they will be at the other end quickly. They are to tell him that the enemy has <hi type="italic">seized the passes</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.32">v. 32</reference>), the forts or blockades upon the river, and that, having got over the river, he has set fire to the reeds on the river side, to alarm and terrify the city, so that all the men of war are affrighted and have thrown down their arms and surrendered at discretion. The messengers come, like Job's, one upon the heels of another, with these tidings, which are immediately confirmed with a witness by the enemies' being in the palace and slaying the king himself, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.30">Dan. v. 30</reference>. That profane feast which they were celebrating at the very time when the city was taken, which was both an evidence of their strange security and a great advantage to the enemy, seems here to be referred to (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.38-Jer.51.39">v. 38, 39</reference>): <hi type="italic">They shall roar together like lions,</hi> as men in their revels do, when the wine has got into their heads. They call it <hi type="italic">singing;</hi> but in scripture-language, and in the language of sober men, it is called <hi type="italic">yelling like lions' whelps.</hi> It is probable that they were drinking confusion to Cyrus and his army with loud huzzas. Well, says God, in their heat, when they are inflamed (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.11">Isa. v. 11</reference>) and their heads are hot with hard drinking, I will <hi type="italic">make their feasts,</hi> I will <hi type="italic">give them their portion.</hi> They have passed their cup round; now <hi type="italic">the cup of the Lord's right hand shall be turned unto them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.15-Hab.2.16">Hab. ii. 15, 16</reference>), a cup of fury, which shall <hi type="italic">make them drunk that they may rejoice</hi> (or rather <hi type="italic">that they may revel it</hi>) and <hi type="italic">sleep a perpetual sleep;</hi> let them be as merry as they can with that bitter cup, but it shall lay them to sleep never to wake more (as <reference osisRef="Jer.51.57">v. 57</reference>); for <hi type="italic">on that night,</hi> in the midst of the jollity, was <hi type="italic">Belshazzar slain.</hi> 6. It is to be a universal destruction. God will make thorough work of it; for, as he will perform what he has purposed, so he will perfect what he has begun. <hi type="italic">The slain shall fall</hi> in great abundance throughout <hi type="italic">the land of the Chaldeans;</hi> multitudes shall be <hi type="italic">thrust through in her streets,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.51.4">v. 4</reference>. They are <hi type="italic">brought down like lambs to the slaughter</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.40">v. 40</reference>), in such great numbers, so easily, and the enemies make no more of killing them than the butcher does of killing lambs. The strength of the enemy, and their invading them, are here compared to an irruption and inundation of waters (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.42">v. 42</reference>): <hi type="italic">The sea has come up upon Babylon,</hi> which, when it has once broken through its bounds, there is no fence against, so that she is <hi type="italic">covered with the multitude of its waves,</hi> overpowered by a numerous army; <hi type="italic">her cities</hi> then become <hi type="italic">a desolation,</hi> an uninhabited uncultivated desert, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.43">v. 43</reference>. 7. It is a destruction that shall reach the gods of Babylon, the idols and images, and fall with a particular weight upon them. "In token that <hi type="italic">the whole land shall be confounded</hi> and all <hi type="italic">her slain shall fall</hi> and that throughout all the country <hi type="italic">the wounded shall groan, I will do judgment upon her graven images,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Jer.51.47">v. 47</reference> and again <reference osisRef="Jer.51.52">v. 52</reference>. All must needs perish if their gods perish, from whom they expect protection. Though the invaders are themselves idolaters, yet they shall destroy the images and temples of the gods of Babylon, as an earnest of the abolishing of all counterfeit deities. Bel was the principal idol that the Babylonians worshipped, and therefore that is by name here marked for destruction (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.44">v. 44</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will punish Bel,</hi> that great devourer, that image to which such abundance of sacrifices are offered and such rich spoils dedicated, and to whose temple there is such a vast resort. He shall disgorge what he has so greedily regaled himself with. God will bring forth out of his temple all the wealth laid up there, <reference osisRef="Job.20.15">Job xx. 15</reference>. His altars shall be forsaken, none shall regard him any more, and so that idol which was thought to be a wall to Babylon shall fall and fail them. 8. It shall be a final destruction. You may <hi type="italic">take balm for her pain,</hi> but in vain; she that <hi type="italic">would not be healed</hi> by the word of God <hi type="italic">shall not be healed</hi> by his providence, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.8-Jer.51.9">v. 8, 9</reference>. <hi type="italic">Babylon</hi> shall <hi type="italic">become heaps</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.37">v. 37</reference>), and, to complete its infamy, no use shall be made even of the ruins of Babylon, so execrable shall they be, and attended with such ill omens (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.26">v. 26</reference>): <hi type="italic">They shall not take of thee a stone for a corner, nor a stone for foundations.</hi> People shall not care for having any thing to do with Babylon, or whatever belonged to it. Or it denotes that there shall be nothing left in Babylon on which to ground any hopes or attempts of raising it into a kingdom again; for, as it follows here, <hi type="italic">it shall be desolate for ever.</hi> St. Jerome says that in his time, though the ruins of Babylon's walls were to be seen, yet the ground enclosed by them was a forest of wild beasts. <div eID="gen18221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18222" type="x-p"/> IX. Here is a call to God's people to go out of Babylon. It is their wisdom, when the ruin is approaching, to quit the city and retire into the country (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.6">v. 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Flee out of the midst of Babylon,</hi> and get into some remote corner, that you may save your lives, and may not be cut off in her iniquity." When God's judgments are abroad it is good to get as far as we can from those against whom they are levelled, as Israel from the tents of Korah. This agrees with the advice Christ gave his disciples, with reference to the destruction of Jerusalem. <hi type="italic">Let those who shall be in Judea flee to the mountains,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.24.16">Matt. xxiv. 16</reference>. It is their wisdom to <hi type="italic">get out of the midst of Babylon,</hi> lest they be involved, if not in her ruins, yet in her fears (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.45-Jer.51.46">v. 45, 46</reference>): <hi type="italic">Lest your heart faint, and you fear for the rumour that shall be heard in the land.</hi> Though God had told them that Cyrus should be their deliverer, and Babylon's destruction their deliverance, yet they had been told also that <hi type="italic">in the peace there of they should have peace,</hi> and therefore the alarms given to Babylon would put them into a fright, and perhaps they might not have faith and consideration enough to suppress those fears, for which reason they are here advised to get out of the hearing of the alarms. Note, Those who have not grace enough to keep their temper in temptation should have wisdom enough to keep out of the way of temptation. But this is not all; it is not only their wisdom to quit the city when the ruin is approaching, but it is their duty to quit the country too when the ruin is accomplished, and they are set at liberty by the pulling down of the prison over their heads. This they are told, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.50-Jer.51.51">v. 50, 51</reference>: "<hi type="italic">You</hi> Israelites, <hi type="italic">who have escaped the sword of the Chaldeans</hi> your oppressors, and of the Persians their destroyers, now that the year of release has come, <hi type="italic">go away, stand not still;</hi> hasten to your own country again, however you may be comfortably seated in Babylon, for this is not your rest, but Canaan is." 1. He puts them in mind of the inducements they had to return: "<hi type="italic">Remember the Lord afar off,</hi> his presence with you now, though you are here afar off from your native soil; his presence with your fathers formerly in the temple, though you are now afar off from the ruins of it." How is that city surprised and become an <hi type="italic">astonishment among the nations</hi> that was the praise, and glory, and admiration of the whole earth!" Babylon's ruin is Zion's praise.
